title: Pressure Direction
shortDefinition: Effective pressure has a specific direction: diagonal, to far hip, to shoulder line, or down through hip line.
whyItMatters: Straight-down pressure often lets opponents frame or hip escape; diagonal pressure makes them lose direction.
deepExplanation: Pressure direction links head, sternum, pelvis, knees, and toes. When they do not point together, you feel heavy but do not control.
beginnerView: Ask where your force is going.
advancedView: Change pressure direction to make frames point the wrong way, then pass or pin.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Pressure Direction during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Pressure Direction to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Pressure Direction is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Pressure Direction before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
